original_value: AbstractDamping determines how the energy in dynamic deformations is dissipated. The design of damping requires models where the behavior along deformation modes is easily controlled, while other motions are left unaffected. In this paper, we propose a framework for the design of damping using dissipation potentials formulated as functions of strain rate. We study simple parameterizations of the models, the application to continuum and discrete deformation models, and practical implications for implementation. We also study previous simple damping models, in particular we demonstrate limitations of Rayleigh damping. We analyze in detail the application of strain rate dissipation potentials to two highly different deformation models, StVK hyperlasticity and yarn‐level cloth with sliding persistent contacts. These deformation models are representative of the range of applicability of the damping model.

result.paraphrase: AbstractDamping governs how energy from dynamic deformations is dissipated. Designing damping calls for models that let deformation modes be controlled readily while leaving other motions unchanged. In this paper, we present a damping-design framework based on dissipation potentials expressed as functions of strain rate. We examine simple model parameterizations, applications to both continuum and discrete deformation models, and implementation implications in practice. We also review earlier simple damping models, highlighting the limitations of Rayleigh damping. In detail, we analyze strain-rate dissipation potentials for two very different deformation models: StVK hyperlasticity and yarn-level cloth with sliding persistent contacts. These cases represent the scope of the damping model’s applicability.
